opus-5.5.text:
I think we're going to see a real shift from the current phase, where enterprises run a lot of experiments and pilots, toward a smaller set of deeply integrated deployments that drive real value.

Right now there's a proliferation of point solutions: a tool for summarizing contracts, another for customer support, another for writing marketing copy. Many of them are useful, but they sit on the periphery of the business. Over time I expect enterprises to consolidate. They'll want fewer vendors and systems that plug directly into their data, workflows and security posture, rather than dozens of disconnected apps each holding a slice of their information.

The second shift is from assistants to agents. The early wave was largely chat: you ask a question and get an answer. The next wave is systems that take action. They pull from your CRM, reconcile something in your ERP, draft a response, route it for approval and close the loop. That's where the productivity gains really show up, but it also raises the bar on reliability, auditability and control. Enterprises won't hand over consequential workflows to something they can't inspect or govern.

That's also why I think deployment flexibility matters so much. Many of the most valuable use cases are in regulated industries like finance, healthcare, government and telecom, where the data is sensitive and can't just be shipped off to a third-party API. Being able to run models privately, on-prem or in your own VPC, customized to your domain, is a prerequisite for those organizations.

On specialization, I think the answer is "both." You'll have strong general-purpose foundation models underneath, and then a lot of value created by adapting them to a specific domain, company and workflow. The specialized application layer won't disappear. It will become more about deep integration and domain knowledge than about wrapping a model with a nice interface.

So the trajectory is from novelty, to point solutions, to AI woven into the core operations of the business. We're somewhere in the middle of that transition now, and I think the next couple of years are when it really starts to show up in the numbers.

r001.rationale: The response predicts consolidation from a proliferation of point solutions toward fewer vendors and systems.

r002.rationale: It says agents may draw on both CRM and ERP, but does not clearly state that departmental agents need information beyond their department’s primary business application.

r003.rationale: It cites disconnected apps and fragmented information as reasons to consolidate, but does not identify the burden of connecting many apps to enterprise data sources as a driver.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we're still early, and the pattern we're seeing at Cohere is that enterprises start narrow and then expand outward.

The first wave was almost always some flavor of retrieval. Take the mountain of internal documents, contracts, support tickets, policies, and let people actually ask questions against it. That's the entry point because it's low risk, the value is obvious, and it doesn't require the model to take any action in the world. You're just making knowledge accessible.

What's happening now is that once that works, people get more ambitious. They want the model to not just answer the question but do the thing. Open the ticket, draft the response, reconcile the two records, kick off the workflow. So you move from search and summarization into agents that are embedded in actual business processes. And that's where the specialization really matters, because a generic model that's never seen your schema, your jargon, your approval chains, is going to stumble. The winners there are the applications that are deeply fitted to a domain: a model that understands financial filings, or clinical notes, or telecom network logs, and has been tuned on that.

Longer term, I think specialization and generality converge in a slightly counterintuitive way. The base capability gets commoditized and very cheap. What becomes valuable is the layer around it: the proprietary data, the fine-tuning, the tools the model can call, the guardrails, and the deployment story. Enterprises care enormously about where their data lives and who can see it. So you end up with a lot of private, on-prem or VPC deployments of models that are customized to a company and quietly running hundreds of small, boring, incredibly valuable tasks.

The thing I'd caution against is the idea that this is one big chatbot in the corner of the screen. The real evolution is toward AI that's mostly invisible, woven into existing systems, doing work that nobody wants to do, and getting measured on whether it moved a business metric rather than whether it impressed someone in a demo.

r001.rationale: The response describes adoption expanding from narrow retrieval use cases into workflows, but does not predict a shift from team-level purchases toward consolidation.

r002.rationale: It mentions agents using company documents, schemas, and workflows, but does not state that departmental agents need information beyond their department’s primary business application.

r003.rationale: The response discusses data, tools, and deployment, but does not identify the maintenance burden of connecting separate AI applications to enterprise data sources as a reason to consolidate.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see enterprises move from experimenting with general-purpose chatbots to deploying applications that are very specific to the work they do. A chatbot is a useful entry point, but it still puts a lot of the burden on the user to figure out how to get value from it. A specialized application can bring together the right information, the right tools, and the steps needed to complete a task.

That doesn’t necessarily mean every application needs its own model. You can have a broadly capable model underneath, with specialization coming from the data it can access and the workflow around it. Over time, I’d expect more of the AI to disappear into the software people already use. The question becomes less ‘What can I ask this model?’ and more ‘Can this system reliably help me get this piece of work done?’

r001.rationale: The response predicts a shift from general-purpose chatbots to specialized applications, but does not describe decentralized team purchases moving toward consolidation.

r002.rationale: It mentions bringing together relevant information and tools, but does not state that departmental agents need information beyond the department’s primary business application.

r003.rationale: It does not mention the maintenance burden of connecting separate AI applications to enterprise data sources or identify that burden as a reason to consolidate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see enterprises move from experimenting with general-purpose chat interfaces to deploying applications built around specific workflows. A tool for a lawyer needs to behave differently from a tool for someone in customer support. They need different information, different integrations, and different ways of checking whether the output is good enough.

The underlying models may be broadly capable, but the application has to understand the context of the business. What data can this person access? What actions are they allowed to take? When should it ask for a human to review something?

Over time, I think those applications will become more capable of actually carrying out work. You might start with a system that helps draft a response, then move to one that can resolve a routine request end to end. That progression will depend on earning trust through reliable performance on fairly specific tasks.
